bridges.statement: Cosmological, moral, and historical evidence cumulatively warrants belief in the Christian God revealed in Christ.
Contingent and changing reality points to a necessary, immaterial, purely actual divine cause.
Apparently gratuitous suffering is compatible with an omniscient and omnipotent God who has greater-good reasons and brings creation toward perfection.
Objective moral obligation, responsibility, and intrinsic human dignity are better explained by theism than by emotivism.
Divine hiddenness can preserve epistemic and cognitive freedom, while sincere error need not itself incur condemnation.
Christianity is evidentially accountable because historical and philosophical findings could defeat its constituent claims.
The total evidence, especially suffering and hiddenness, does not warrant Christian belief even though some Christian evidence modestly raises its credibility.
The extent and evolutionary embedding of suffering are more expected under atheism than under a benevolent creator.
Sincere nonresistant nonbelief conflicts with the existence of a perfectly loving God able to provide noncoercive disclosure.
The problem of evil can operate as an internal critique of Christian morality without requiring the skeptic to affirm objective moral facts.
Evidence can increase Christianity's credibility without raising it enough to make Christian belief warranted overall.
